patterns: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
explanation: You tried to join a string (text) with a whole number using +. Python cannot mix text and numbers this way.
suggestion: Convert the number to text with str(), for example: "hello" + str(5). Or use an f-string: f"hello {5}".

patterns: can only concatenate str (not "float") to str
explanation: You tried to join a string (text) with a decimal number using +. Python cannot mix text and numbers this way.
suggestion: Convert the number to text with str(), for example: "price: " + str(9.99). Or use an f-string: f"price: {9.99}".

patterns: can only concatenate list (not "tuple") to list
explanation: You tried to join a list with a tuple using +. These are two different kinds of collections and cannot be added directly.
suggestion: Convert the tuple to a list first with list(my_tuple), then add them: my_list + list(my_tuple). Or use extend() if you want to change the original list.

explanation: You tried to add a number and a string with +. Python does not know how to add a number and text together.
suggestion: If you want to join them as text, convert the number: str(5) + " apples". If you want to do math, make sure both sides are numbers.

explanation: You tried to subtract one string from another with -. You can only subtract numbers, not text.
suggestion: Check that both sides of the - are numbers. If you meant to remove part of a string, use methods like replace() or slicing instead.

explanation: You tried to loop over a whole number. A single number has no items to step through.
suggestion: Loop over a list, a string, or a range instead. Example: for i in range(5): not for i in 5:.

explanation: You tried to loop over None. None is empty and has nothing to loop over.
suggestion: Make sure the variable holds a list or string before the loop. A function may have returned None by accident.

explanation: You tried to loop over a decimal number. A single number cannot be stepped through item by item.
suggestion: Make sure you are looping over a list, string, or range, not a float value.

explanation: You tried to loop over a True/False value. A boolean has only one value and cannot be stepped through.
suggestion: Check the variable you are looping over. It should be a list, string, or other collection, not True or False.

explanation: You put () after a list name, as if the list were a function. Lists cannot be called.
suggestion: Remove the (). If you want an item from the list, use square brackets: my_list[0].

explanation: You put () after a string name, as if the string were a function. Strings cannot be called.
suggestion: Remove the (). Check that you did not overwrite a function name with a string by accident.

explanation: You put parentheses () after a dictionary name, as if it were a function. Dictionaries are not functions.
suggestion: Remove the (). To get a value from a dictionary use square brackets: my_dict["key"].

explanation: You tried to call something that is None (as if it were a function). None cannot be called with ().
suggestion: Check that the variable holds a real function before you call it. A previous assignment or function may have set it to None.

explanation: You used square brackets [] on a whole number. Numbers do not contain items you can pick by position.
suggestion: Only use [] on lists, strings, or dictionaries. You may have replaced a list with a number earlier in the code.

explanation: You used square brackets [] on None. None has no items to look up.
suggestion: Check that the variable is not None before using []. A function may have returned None.

explanation: You used square brackets [] on a set. Sets do not keep order and do not support looking up items by index.
suggestion: Convert the set to a list first if you need indexing: list(my_set)[0]. Or loop over the set instead of using an index.

patterns: object of type 'int' has no len()
explanation: You asked for the length of a whole number with len(). Only things that contain items (lists, strings, etc.) have a length.
suggestion: Make sure you call len() on a list, string, or dictionary, not on a number.

patterns: object of type 'float' has no len()
explanation: You asked for the length of a decimal number with len(). Only things that contain items (lists, strings, etc.) have a length.
suggestion: Make sure you call len() on a list, string, or dictionary, not on a float.

explanation: You called a function but left out one or more required inputs.
suggestion: Look at the function definition (the def line). Count the required names inside the parentheses and pass that many values when you call it. Example: if def greet(name): then call greet("Ada").

explanation: You gave a function more inputs than it is allowed to take.
suggestion: Look at the function definition and pass only the number of values it expects. Remove any extra values from the call.

patterns: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
explanation: You tried to change an item inside a tuple. Tuples cannot be changed after they are created (they are immutable).
suggestion: If you need to change items, use a list instead of a tuple. Convert with list(my_tuple), make the change, then convert back if needed.

patterns: 'str' object does not support item assignment
explanation: You tried to change a character inside a string. Strings cannot be changed after they are created.
suggestion: Build a new string instead. For example use replace() or slicing: new_str = old_str[:2] + "X" + old_str[3:].

patterns: 'bytes' object does not support item assignment
explanation: You tried to change a byte inside a bytes object. Bytes objects cannot be changed after they are created.
suggestion: Convert to a bytearray if you need to modify it: ba = bytearray(my_bytes), then change items, then convert back with bytes(ba).

explanation: You called strip() with an argument, but the version of strip you used does not accept any.
suggestion: Call strip() with empty parentheses: my_string.strip(). If you want to remove specific characters, check the documentation for the correct way on your Python version.

patterns: append() takes exactly one argument (2 given)
explanation: You called list.append() with more than one value. append() only accepts a single item.
suggestion: Pass only one item: my_list.append(value). To add several items at once use extend([a, b, c]) or += [a, b, c].

patterns: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not int
explanation: A function that needs a file path received a number instead. File paths must be text (strings).
suggestion: Pass the path as a string, for example open("data.txt") or open(str(my_number)) if you really need to turn a number into a path name.

patterns: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not NoneType
explanation: A function that needs a file path received None instead. File paths must be text (strings), not empty.
suggestion: Make sure the path variable is set to a real string before you use it. Check that no earlier code set it to None.

patterns: isinstance() arg 2 must be a type, a tuple of types, or a union
explanation: The second argument to isinstance() must be a type (like int or str) or a tuple of types. You gave it something else.
suggestion: Write isinstance(value, int) or isinstance(value, (int, float)). Do not put a string or an instance there.

explanation: You used a name (variable or function) that Python does not know. It was never created, is spelled wrong, or is used too early.
suggestion: 1) Check the spelling. 2) Make sure you give the name a value before you use it (example: user_id = 42). 3) If it comes from another file, add the correct import line.

patterns: list assignment index out of range
explanation: You used a position number that does not exist. Positions start at 0. If a list has 3 items, the last valid position is 2.
suggestion: Check the length with len(my_list). Only use numbers from 0 to len(my_list)-1. Example: my_list[0] is the first item.

explanation: You called .pop() on a list that has zero items. There is nothing to take out.
suggestion: Only call pop() when the list has items. Safe way: if my_list: item = my_list.pop()

explanation: You asked a dictionary for a key that is not inside it.
suggestion: Check the spelling and capital letters of the key. Safer options: use my_dict.get('key') (returns None if missing) or write if 'key' in my_dict: before accessing it.

patterns: invalid literal for int() with base 10
explanation: You tried to turn some text into a whole number with int(), but the text is not a valid whole number (it may contain letters, a decimal point, or be empty).
suggestion: Make sure the text only contains digits (0-9) and an optional minus sign. If it may have a decimal, use float() first or clean the text before converting.

patterns: could not convert string to float
explanation: You tried to turn some text into a decimal number with float(), but the text is not a valid number.
suggestion: Check that the text looks like a number (for example '3.14' or '42'). Remove any letters, spaces, or special words like 'N/A' before converting.

explanation: You asked a math function (like sqrt or log) to do something that is not allowed with the number you gave (for example square root of a negative number).
suggestion: Check the input value. Many math functions only work with positive numbers or numbers in a certain range. Add a check before calling the function.

explanation: You tried to find or remove a piece of text that does not exist inside the string.
suggestion: Check the exact spelling and case of the substring. Use 'in' to test first: if 'abc' in my_string: before calling find or index methods that raise errors.

explanation: You tried to remove a value from a list, but that value is not in the list.
suggestion: Check that the item really exists before removing it: if x in my_list: my_list.remove(x). Or use a try/except if you expect it might be missing.

explanation: You tried to unpack a sequence into fewer variables than the number of items it contains (for example a, b = [1, 2, 3]).
suggestion: Make the number of variables match the number of items, or use * to collect extras: a, b, *rest = my_list.

explanation: You tried to unpack a sequence into more variables than the number of items it contains (for example a, b = [1]).
suggestion: Make the number of variables match the number of items, or give a default for missing ones. Check the length of the sequence first.

explanation: You tried to call a method on something that is None (empty). None has no methods or properties.
suggestion: Before using the variable, check that it is not None. Example: if result is not None: result.get('key'). A function may have returned None by mistake.

explanation: You tried to use a method or property that this kind of object does not have. For example, calling .lower() on a list or .append() on a string.
suggestion: Print the variable and check its type with type(my_var). Then only use methods that belong to that type. Also double-check the method name for typos.

explanation: You tried to divide a number by zero (or take the remainder with % zero). Division by zero is not allowed.
suggestion: Check that the number you are dividing by is not zero before doing the division. Add a simple if denominator != 0: guard.

explanation: Python looked for a file or folder and could not find it at the path you wrote.
suggestion: 1) Check the spelling of the file name. 2) Make sure the file really exists. 3) Run the program from the right folder, or use the full path (example: /home/user/data.csv).

explanation: Python tried to open or change a file but your user account does not have permission to do that.
suggestion: Check the file permissions. You may need to run as administrator, change the file's permissions, or choose a different folder you are allowed to write to.

explanation: You treated a folder as if it were a file (for example trying to open a directory with open()).
suggestion: Use a file path that points to an actual file, not a folder. If you need to work with the folder contents, use os.listdir() or pathlib instead.

explanation: You treated a regular file as if it were a folder (for example trying to list its contents like a directory).
suggestion: Make sure the path points to a real folder, not a file. Check the path with os.path.isdir() if needed.

explanation: You tried to create a file or folder that already exists, and the operation does not allow overwriting.
suggestion: Choose a different name, delete the existing file first, or use a mode that allows overwriting (for example open(..., 'w')).

explanation: Python cannot find the library (module) you tried to import. It is missing or the name is spelled wrong.
suggestion: Install it with pip. Example: pip install requests. Then check the spelling of the import line (import requests).

explanation: The module itself was found, but the specific name you asked for inside it does not exist (or is spelled wrong).
suggestion: Check the exact spelling of the name after 'import'. Look at the module docs or source to see the real names it provides.

explanation: You used a variable inside a function before giving it a value in that function. Python treats it as a local variable because you assign to it somewhere in the function.
suggestion: Make sure every local variable is assigned a value before you read it. If you meant to use a global variable, add a global statement, or pass the value in as an argument.

explanation: A function kept calling itself (or a chain of functions kept calling each other) so many times that Python stopped it to prevent a crash.
suggestion: Check that your recursive function has a clear stopping condition (base case) that is eventually reached. Make sure the problem gets smaller on each call.

explanation: A generator finished by raising StopIteration, and that exception was not handled the way modern Python expects.
suggestion: Use a for loop to consume the generator, or catch StopIteration yourself. Avoid raising StopIteration directly inside a generator in new code.

explanation: You asked an iterator (like next()) for the next item after it had already finished. There are no more items.
suggestion: Use a for loop when possible, or catch StopIteration, or check that the iterator still has items before calling next().

patterns: int too large to convert to float
explanation: A number became so large that Python could not convert or handle it in the way you asked (for example turning a huge integer into a float).
suggestion: Use smaller numbers, or keep the value as an integer if possible. Check for calculations that grow without limit.

explanation: An assert statement failed. The condition you wrote after assert was False.
suggestion: Look at the assert line and figure out why the condition is not true. Fix the logic or the data that made the assertion fail.

explanation: Python tried to read text using one encoding (usually utf-8) but the file contains bytes that do not match that encoding.
suggestion: Open the file with the correct encoding, for example open(..., encoding='latin-1') or encoding='utf-8'. You can also try encoding='utf-8-sig' or errors='ignore' while debugging.

explanation: Python tried to write text using an encoding that cannot represent some of the characters (for example trying to save emoji with ascii).
suggestion: Use a wider encoding such as utf-8 when writing the file: open(..., encoding='utf-8'). Avoid ascii for text that may contain non-English characters.

patterns: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes
explanation: Python tried to read JSON text but the text is not valid JSON (missing commas, wrong quotes, extra data, or empty).
suggestion: Check the JSON text carefully. Use double quotes for keys and strings, remove trailing commas, and make sure brackets match. You can test the text at jsonlint.com.

explanation: You ran an SQL query that refers to a table that does not exist in the database.
suggestion: Check the table name spelling. Make sure you have created the table (CREATE TABLE) before querying it, and that you are connected to the correct database file.

explanation: You ran an SQL query that refers to a column that does not exist in the table.
suggestion: Check the column name spelling and that it really exists in that table. Use PRAGMA table_info(table_name) to see the real columns.

explanation: The database rejected your change because it would break a rule (for example inserting a duplicate unique value or a NULL into a required column).
suggestion: Check the data you are inserting. Make sure unique fields are not duplicated and that required (NOT NULL) fields always have a value.

explanation: Your regular expression pattern is invalid (for example unmatched parentheses or a bad quantifier).
suggestion: Check the regex pattern carefully. Make sure every ( has a matching ), and that special characters are escaped with \ when you mean them literally.

explanation: The web server returned an error status code (such as 404 Not Found) for your HTTP request.
suggestion: Check the URL spelling and that the resource exists. Look at response.status_code and response.text for more details from the server.

explanation: Python could not connect to the server (network problem, wrong host, or the server is down).
suggestion: Check your internet connection, the URL host name, and that the server is running. Try the URL in a browser to confirm it is reachable.

explanation: The HTTP request took too long and was cancelled because it exceeded the timeout limit.
suggestion: Increase the timeout value if the server is slow, or check whether the server is reachable and responding. Handle the timeout so your program does not crash.

explanation: You tried to unpack (split) a value into several variables, but the value is None. None cannot be unpacked.
suggestion: Make sure the value is a list or tuple before unpacking. Example: a, b = my_list  only works if my_list is not None.

explanation: You used square brackets [] on a method or function. Methods and functions are not lists or dictionaries, so you cannot pick items from them with [].
suggestion: Call the method or function with parentheses first, for example result = my_obj.method(). Then use [] on the result if needed.

explanation: You tried to use a list, dictionary, or set as a key in another dictionary (or put it inside a set). Only simple unchanging values like numbers and strings can be used as keys.
suggestion: Convert the list to a tuple first (tuples can be keys): my_dict[tuple(my_list)] = value. Or use a string or number as the key instead.

patterns: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
'>' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
'<=' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
'>=' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
explanation: You tried to compare text (a string) with a number using < or >. Python cannot decide which is larger when the types are different.
suggestion: Make both sides the same type. Convert the string to a number with int() or float(), or convert the number to text with str().

explanation: You put a minus sign in front of a string (text). The minus sign only works with numbers.
suggestion: If the text holds a number, convert it first: -int(my_string) or -float(my_string). Otherwise remove the minus sign.

patterns: 'in ' requires string as left operand, not int
explanation: You used the word 'in' with a number on the left side. When checking if text contains something, the left side must be a string.
suggestion: Put a string on the left of 'in'. Example: if 'a' in my_string:  not  if 5 in my_string: (unless my_string is a list of numbers).

patterns: argument of type 'int' is not iterable
explanation: You used a whole number where Python expected something you can loop over or search inside (like a list or string).
suggestion: Pass a list, string, or other collection instead of a plain number. Check the value you are giving to the function or to the 'in' operator.

patterns: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable
explanation: You used None where Python expected something you can loop over or search inside. None is empty.
suggestion: Make sure the value is a list or string before using it with 'in' or a loop. A function may have returned None.

explanation: You asked a dictionary for a number key that does not exist. Dictionaries only return values for keys that were actually stored.
suggestion: Check that the number key really exists. Use my_dict.get(0) if you want None instead of an error, or write if 0 in my_dict: first.

explanation: You used square brackets [] on a value that does not support them. Only lists, strings, tuples, and dictionaries allow picking items with [].
suggestion: Check the type of the variable with type(my_var). Only use [] on lists, strings, tuples, or dictionaries.

explanation: You called a string method like split() with an empty separator (''). Python does not allow an empty separator.
suggestion: Pass a real separator such as a space or comma: my_string.split(' ') or my_string.split(','). If you want every character, use list(my_string) instead.

explanation: You tried to read or write a file after it was already closed.
suggestion: Do all reading and writing before you close the file. Best practice: use a with open(...) as f: block so the file closes automatically when you finish.

explanation: Your program tried to use more memory than the computer can give. This often happens with very large lists or endless loops that keep adding data.
suggestion: Process data in smaller pieces instead of loading everything at once. Check for loops that grow a list without limit.

explanation: Python expected the next line to be indented (moved to the right) because of a colon (:) on the line above, but the indent is missing.
A line is indented further than Python expected. Extra spaces or a Tab at the start of the line caused this.
suggestion: Remove the extra spaces or Tab at the beginning of the line so it lines up with the code around it.

patterns: unindent does not match any outer indentation level
explanation: The spaces (or Tabs) used to go back to a previous level do not match any earlier indent. Mixing Tabs and spaces often causes this.
suggestion: Use only spaces (4 spaces per level) for the whole file. Most editors have a setting to convert Tabs to spaces. Make sure the line lines up with an earlier block.

patterns: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation
explanation: Some lines are indented with Tabs and others with spaces. Python does not allow mixing them.
suggestion: Pick one style and use it everywhere. The usual choice is 4 spaces. In your editor, turn on 'convert tabs to spaces' and re-indent the file.

explanation: Python found text that does not follow the language rules (a missing colon, a wrong symbol, or a typo).
suggestion: Look at the line shown in the error. Check for missing colons (:), unmatched brackets, or misspelled keywords. Fix the line and try again.

explanation: Python reached the end of the file while still expecting more code (often a missing closing parenthesis, bracket, or quote).
suggestion: Check that every (, [, { and quote has a matching closing partner. Count them carefully on the lines above the error.

explanation: The code contains a character that Python does not understand in that place (sometimes a fancy quote or symbol copied from a website).
suggestion: Replace any special quotes (“ ”) with normal ones (" "). Remove or replace any odd symbols that do not belong in Python code.

explanation: In Python 3, print is a function and needs parentheses. Writing print "hello" is the old Python 2 style and no longer works.
suggestion: Add parentheses: print("hello") instead of print "hello".

explanation: The program was stopped by you (usually by pressing Ctrl+C).
suggestion: This is not a bug. If you did not mean to stop the program, just run it again. To handle Ctrl+C gracefully you can use a try/except KeyboardInterrupt block.

explanation: A generator was closed before it finished. This is normal when the program no longer needs more values from it.
suggestion: Usually you can ignore this. If you see it unexpectedly, check that you are not closing or deleting a generator while it is still being used.

explanation: You tried to join text (a string) with a number using +. Python cannot mix text and numbers this way.
suggestion: Convert the number to text first: "score: " + str(10). Or use an f-string: f"score: {10}".

patterns: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float'
can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'str'
can't multiply sequence by non-int of type
explanation: You tried to multiply a list or string by something that is not a whole number. Python only allows multiplying a sequence by an integer (to repeat it).
suggestion: Use a whole number on the right side, for example my_list * 3. If you meant math on numbers, make sure both sides are numbers, not a list or string.

patterns: 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
'str' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
cannot be interpreted as an integer
explanation: A function needed a whole number (integer) but you gave it a decimal or some text instead.
suggestion: Pass a whole number. If you have a decimal, convert it with int(my_float). If you have text that looks like a number, use int(my_string).

patterns: order must be str, not int
explanation: A function expected the word for sort order (like 'ascending') as text, but you gave a number instead.
suggestion: Pass a string such as "asc" or "desc", not a number. Check the function documentation for the exact values it accepts.

explanation: A function expected text (a string or bytes) but received something else.
suggestion: Pass a string or bytes object. Convert other values with str() or bytes() if needed.

patterns: descriptor '.*' requires a '.*' object but received a
explanation: You used a method in a special way that expects an instance of a class, but you gave it a different kind of object (or used it on the class itself).
suggestion: Call the method on an instance of the correct class, for example my_obj.method(), not on the class or on the wrong type.

patterns: must be called with .* instance as first argument
explanation: You called a method without an instance of the class. In older Python this is called an unbound method error.
suggestion: Create an object first, then call the method on it: obj = MyClass(); obj.method(). Or use MyClass.method(obj) if you must call it on the class.

explanation: You asked a dictionary for the key None, False, or True, but that key is not in the dictionary.
suggestion: Check whether you really meant to use None/True/False as a key. Use my_dict.get(None) if you want None instead of an error when the key is missing.

patterns: max() arg is an empty sequence
min() arg is an empty sequence
explanation: You called max() or min() on an empty list (or other empty collection). There is no largest or smallest value when there are no items.
suggestion: Check that the list is not empty before calling max() or min(). Example: if my_list: biggest = max(my_list)

patterns: zero length field name in format
explanation: In an f-string or .format() call you left an empty set of braces {}. Python needs a name or value inside the braces.
suggestion: Put a variable or expression inside the braces. Example: f"Hello {name}" instead of f"Hello {}".

explanation: You used a format code (the part after : inside braces) that does not work with that kind of value. For example using a number format on text.
suggestion: Check the format specifier. Common ones: :.2f for 2 decimal places on a number, :s for strings. Make sure the value type matches the code you chose.

explanation: Python found the module but could not load a required system library (DLL) that the module needs. This is common on Windows with packages that use C extensions.
suggestion: Reinstall the package (pip uninstall package_name then pip install package_name). Make sure you have the correct Visual C++ redistributable installed if the error mentions it. Try installing a binary wheel that matches your Python version.

explanation: A string was started with a quote but never closed before the end of the line. Python reached the end of the line while still inside the string.
suggestion: Add the missing closing quote on the same line, or use triple quotes for a multi-line string: """text""".

patterns: unexpected character after line continuation character
explanation: You used a backslash (\) to continue a line, but something other than a newline came right after it.
suggestion: Put the backslash at the very end of the line with nothing after it (not even a space). Or wrap the expression in parentheses so you do not need the backslash.

explanation: A parenthesis, square bracket, or curly brace was opened but never closed, or an extra closing one was found.
suggestion: Count the (, [, { and their closing partners. Make sure every opener has a matching closer in the right order.

explanation: The code contains a hidden or special character that Python cannot use in that place (sometimes copied from a website or document).
suggestion: Delete the strange character and type it again by hand. Watch for invisible characters or unusual quotes.

explanation: In a function call you put a normal value after a named argument (like name=...). Once you use a name=, every argument after it must also use a name.
suggestion: Either put all positional values first, or give every argument a name. Example: func(1, 2, c=3) is OK; func(a=1, 2) is not.

explanation: A floating-point math operation failed (for example an invalid calculation with decimal numbers).
suggestion: Check the numbers you are using in the calculation. Avoid dividing by very small values or performing operations that produce infinity or undefined results.

explanation: You tried to await the same coroutine object more than once. After a coroutine has been awaited, it cannot be awaited again.
suggestion: Create a new coroutine each time you need to run the async function. Call the async function again instead of reusing the old coroutine object.

patterns: This event loop is already running
explanation: Async code needs an event loop. Either none is running, or you tried to start one while another is already running.
suggestion: Use asyncio.run(main()) to start your async program. Avoid calling loop.run_until_complete() from inside a running loop; use await instead.

explanation: The program called sys.exit() or raised SystemExit to stop on purpose.
suggestion: This is usually intentional. If you did not mean to exit, look for sys.exit() or raise SystemExit in your code and remove or guard it.

explanation: An operation on a memory buffer failed (for example resizing a buffer that is still being used elsewhere).
suggestion: Make sure no other part of the code is still using the buffer when you try to change or free it.

explanation: You tried to use an object through a weak reference, but the real object has already been deleted.
suggestion: Keep a normal reference to the object if you still need it. Weak references do not stop the object from being cleaned up.
